title: On Compilers and Interpreters (30 November 2025)
text:
I wrote this quick blog-post while I was reviewing Python Functions.
I stumbled upon the following statements as I read the Functions section in Python In a Nutshell by Martelli et.al. (with a few changes for context):

When the Python interpreter (the python executable on your computer) encounters a def statement in your Python script or REPL, it compiles the function body, creating a function object.

This statement subtly describes the dual nature of python (the executable), which is both a compiler and an interpreter. It also prompted me to reexamine compilation and interpretation in the context of programming languages. I had always encountered these terms. I simply asked myself: Do I understand these terms and the difference between them now?
This blog-post answers that question.
First, let’s look up the contemporary dictionary meanings of the two verbs: compile and interpret. I have stated the meanings most relevant to a computing context in a boldface.

Compile (v.): 1) get or gather together (synonym: to accumulate), 2) put together out of existing material (e.g. compile a list), or 3) use a computer program (a “compiler”) to translate source code written in a particular programming language into computer-readable machine code that can be executed.
Interpret (v.): 1) make sense of; assign meaning to (e.g. interpret a message) 2) give rendition of (e.g. a Beethoven sonata) 3) create an image or likeness of (synonym: to represent) 3) restate words from one language into another language (synonym: to translate), or 4) make sense of a language.

Aren’t the relevant definitions confusing? Don’t they mean the same thing (to translate)? Restating (modified slightly to suit Python, but it doesn’t matter) them:

Compile: Use the python executable to translate a complete Python program into the Intel microprocessor’s machine code (instructions) which can be run or executed (actual physical changes occur at the semiconductor level!)
Interpret: Use the python executable to translate or restate the words from Python (e.g. an assignment like x = 20) into another language like Intel microprocessor’s (x86 64) machine code (something like 48 c7 c0 01 00 00 00 encoded in binary). This is like how a human interpreter interprets a foreign president’s response for the native speakers to understand.

When a program runs on a computer, the CPU simply executes corresponding instructions one by one.
Thus, the CPU is the ultimate interpreter or executor which runs the instruction in its machine code. The CPU does not translate the program written in computer’s RAM in a ‘language’ like 48 c7 c0 01 00 00 00 into some other language, but it, like a faithful and unerring servant, “directly makes sense of it” by taking actions (thus interpreting it–See meaning #1 of interpret above).
For a Python program to do anything on a physical machine, therefore, we need two things:

Our Python program’s code translated into a binary machine code (instructions for a CPU).
A CPU that interprets or makes sense of it by taking the instructed actions.

We now have more nuanced definitions: 1) Compile: Translate something from one formal language into another. Formal languages, unlike natural languages, have unambiguous grammars. 2) Interpret: Make sense of (well-defined) instructions in a language by taking actions intended therein.
Until about the 70s (and of course even now), we had a programming language like C in which programmers wrote their programs, a compiler like the gcc (which is itself a big program written in C and compiled into a computer’s machine code) that compiled those C programs into a computer’s machine code, and a machine that interpreted that machine code. A typical workflow was straightforward:

Create a C program file, a.c. This file is not executable.
Compile it: For example, gcc a.c. This creates an executable file a.out which has all the machine instructions. The compiler ensures that a.c is valid C code, and a.out is valid machine code.
Run the executable file: ./a.out which loads the instructions in computer’s memory. We didn’t call this step interpretation, although the computer makes sense of (interprets) those instructions.

This required that different computers had different compilers, although the C program file was the same. You could give your little C program, a.c, to your friend on a floppy, and s/he would compile it on their computer to, say, a.exe, and run it.
What is a compiler like gcc then? Well, it must be an executable file that has all the instructions for the machine. Its job is to take your C program and produce a corresponding executable. There is of course a bootstrapping problem here if gcc were not available as a sequence of machine instructions. If gcc was the name of the executable program that was created by compiling a C (or other language) source program, then we must compile that source program somehow!
Later, the idea of a writing computer programs for a virtual machine came along. That made the term ‘interpreter’ more popular. A compiler translated programs from a source language into an instruction language for the virtual machine. The instructions for the virtual machine were called the bytecode.
The compiler created the bytecode.
An interpreter interpreted (made sense of) the bytecode.
To finally see the physical changes on a real machine, however, interpreter also ran or executed the actual machine code corresponding to the bytecode.
Two notable programming languages in this regard are Python and Java. Let’s consider Python.

title: Hello, World!
text: This is my first blog post, powered by Quarto and GitHub Workflow. I am not exactly happy because it took a half day to set all this up. But now that it is all set up, I can hopefully produce some readable blog-posts that are version-controlled.

title: Hello, World!
text:
My Workflow

Keep my phase-wise notebooks (which are expected to be detailed explorations) up-to-date. I decided not to convert them into a website like this one. Instead, they are just executed notebooks (even with errors to demonstrate something) committed to my GitHub repo.
Just see the individual notebooks in phase-1, phase-2 etc. I link my all my phase-star notebooks from my blog using the GH source links. A typical link is https://github.com/kedarmhaswade/yakk-2/blob/main/phase-1/day10_pretest.ipynb and it should go verbatim in a blog-post.
That is my shortcut to host the notebooks without any explicit hosting overhead! I think it works for me.
When I want to write a blog-post, I come to this folder (/blog of my repository) and create my blog-post also as a notebook (contains mostly Markdown, but may contain some exploration code-blocks too).
I ask quarto to render the static HTML from these “notebooks as blog-posts”. For the same purpose, I utilize a GitHub workflow for static HTML.
After I am done with my blog-post, I render the Quarto website locally and make sure it succeeds and generates the static pages in the _site subfolder of my blog folder.
On commit and push, GitHub runs my workflow and pushes the static HTML (my blog-posts) to this website that you are reading it on.
Simple, eh?
